title: I’m building a trading research platform—how would you evaluate its workflow and data transparency?
author: TradeAnalyzerPr
selftext:
I’m the founder.  
TradeAnalyzer.Pro brings market screening, chart analysis and rule-based strategy research into a shared workspace.  
The problem I’m trying to address is straightforward: finding an interesting instrument is often easier than evaluating the idea consistently.  
The intended process is to shortlist markets, compare timeframes, inspect the chart and document what supports or contradicts the hypothesis.  
The platform covers supported crypto, stock-linked, forex and commodity instruments. Its core research timeframes are 15m, 1h, 4h and 1d.  
There are also separate research tools for reported liquidations and sampled public trader positions. Their coverage matters: neither dataset represents the entire market.  
I would appreciate feedback on three questions:  
What information must a screener show before you investigate a result?  
How should a platform present conflicting readings across timeframes?  
Which assumptions should always appear beside simulation metrics?  
The platform is here:  
https://tradeanalyzer.pro  
Specific criticism around workflow clarity and data transparency would be particularly useful.  
This is a research platform. It does not execute trades or provide personalized financial advice.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
we talked about this a month ago, the swap-the-exit test, good to see it turned into a product.

on your three questions, from running a research desk of my own:

a screener result needs its sample size and its data date before anything else. a signal that fired 4 times is a story, not a result, and a screen built on bars that end yesterday has to say so.

conflicting timeframes: don't resolve them for the user. show each timeframe's reading side by side with the bar count behind it and let the daily disagree with the 15m. the platforms that blend them into one score hide the disagreement, which is the information.

beside every simulation metric: the fill assumption (mid, last, or the touched side), fees, and whether the bar's close was known when the entry fired. the look-ahead question is the one most tools leave out and the one that explains most too-good results.

which of the four timeframes do your users end up trusting when they disagree?
